Glass harmonica tuning

Glass harmonica tuning is the process of adjusting the pitch of the nested glass bowls of a glass harmonica by grinding their rims.[1] Tuners usually work from the largest bowl to the smallest and check each bowl against a reference fork before and after every pass of the grinding wheel.

Because the glass warms during grinding, a bowl that sounds correct at the bench can drift sharp once it cools, so experienced tuners leave each bowl to rest overnight before the final check.[citation needed]

History

[edit]

Early instruments were tuned by ear against a harpsichord, which made the results depend heavily on the tuner and the room. Workshops later adopted sets of tuning forks, and by the middle of the nineteenth century most makers kept a reference set that was checked every season.[2]

Workshop practice

[edit]

A typical workshop session followed a fixed order of steps that apprentices learned before they were allowed near the wheel:

  • Strike the bowl and compare it with the fork.
  • Grind a narrow band of the rim if the bowl is flat.
  • Rest the bowl and repeat the comparison.

The same order is still taught in the few workshops that make the instrument today, although electronic tuners have replaced the forks in most of them.
